title: Shankara bows
hookLine: a great teacher tells an outcaste to move, the outcaste asks one question, and what namaste really bows to
carry: namaste: a bow to the divine in the other
tomorrow: one Upanishad line, two schools: 'you are that,' or 'not that'?
last: THE LETTER THAT DOES NOT PERISH.

lines: MOVE WHAT? THE BODY, OR THE AWARENESS?
ONE SUN, IN THE GANGA AND IN A PUDDLE.
cards: As the tradition tells it, the young teacher Shankara has just bathed in the Ganga at Kashi and is walking to the temple. On the narrow path stands a chandala, a man his society called untouchable, with his dogs.
Shankara tells him: move aside, out of my way. And the man asks a question. Move what?
Should this body, made of food, move away from that body, made of food? Or should the awareness in me move away from the awareness in you?
Is the sun any different shining in the Ganga, or in a puddle in the outcastes' lane? Here's the puzzle: what does Shankara do next?

teach.h: WHOEVER SEES THE ONE IN ALL IS MY TEACHER.
teach.b: The teacher folds his hands to the man he'd just told to move, and the tradition says he answered with five verses, the Manisha Panchakam: whoever sees the one awareness in all, he is my teacher, whatever his birth.

It's the Gita's teaching too: the wise see the same in a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and the one who eats dogs. Now look at the word Hindus say with that same gesture. Namaste looks like one word.

teach.h: NAMAH + TE: A BOW, TO YOU.
teach.b: It's two: namah, a bow, and te, to you. Sandhi is the joining, where words meet and their sounds adjust.
The soft breath at the end of namah, the visarga, meets the t of te, a tooth sound, and moves to the teeth to get ready, becoming s. Namas te: namaste. So namaste isn't hello.

teach.h: A BOW TO THE DIVINE IN THE OTHER.
teach.b: And many Hindus read the bow the way Shankara learned it on that path: palms together at the heart, bowing to the divine that lives in the other person.
That's why children are taught to say it to elders with folded hands, and why it's said to a guest, a teacher, a stranger alike. The joining in the word carries a joining between people.

how: Hindus greet elders, guests and teachers with namaste and folded hands; the story of Shankara and the chandala at Kashi is told with the Manisha Panchakam, five verses traditionally attributed to him.

games.q: on the path at Kashi — tap the pairs.

asked: move the body, or the awareness?

s: namaste is one old word that just means hello
it's two words, namah, a bow, and te, to you: I bow to you.
in the story, Shankara bows to the man he had told to move
the man's question showed him the same awareness in both of them.
the Gita says the wise treat people by their birth
the wise see the same in a priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog and the one who eats dogs.

games.q: your friend says namaste is just a polite way to end a yoga class, like 'bye'. what's the fuller answer?
o: it's namah te, I bow to you, and many Hindus mean a bow to the divine in the other.
she's right; it's only a polite goodbye.
it's a prayer you should only say inside a temple.
games.why: namah, a bow, plus te, to you. with folded hands at the heart, many Hindus read it as Shankara learned on the path: bowing to the divine in the person in front of you.

practice: Fold the hands at the heart. Say namah, then te, slowly, two words; then let them join into namaste.

As you say it, bring to mind someone you'll pass today without really seeing, a cashier, a driver, a neighbor, and bow to them in your mind. If you don't pray, simply wish them well. Then rest the hands and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Sandhi plainly. The joining: where one word's last sound meets the next word's first, and both adjust, the way namah and te become namaste.

orig.note: Sanskrit: namas te, namaḥ, a bow, plus te, to you; the visarga becomes s before t.

carryVoice: Your line: namaste, a bow to the divine in the other. Shankara learned it from the man on the path. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Manisha Panchakam (traditionally attributed to Shankara) and its traditional framing story: Shankara and the chandala at Kashi (body of food and body of food; awareness and awareness; the sun reflected in the Ganga and in a puddle in the outcastes' lane)
Bhagavad Gita 5.18 (the wise see the same in a learned brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater)
namas te (namaḥ + te): visarga before t becomes s (Ashtadhyayi 8.3.34)
